iberia.description: Ferdinand VI’s Spain, steered by the Marqués de la Ensenada, rebuilds fleets and finances under Bourbon centralism; the 1750 Treaty of Madrid redraws the Spanish–Portuguese line in South America. Portugal, rich on Brazilian gold, gets a new king (Joseph I, 1750) and a new strongman, the future Marquis of Pombal—five years before the Lisbon earthquake. Genetics: continuity.

britain.description: Culloden (1746) ends the last Jacobite rising and the clan order of the Highlands. Britain’s parliamentary, debt-financed state pays for a navy that outguns France; Ireland is ruled by a Protestant Ascendancy under the Penal Laws. Hume, Smith and the Scottish Enlightenment flourish; Methodist field preaching spreads. Genetics: continuity.

france.description: Louis XV’s France is Europe’s most populous kingdom and its cultural capital: Montesquieu’s Spirit of the Laws (1748) and the first volume of the Encyclopédie (1751) come out of Paris. The monarchy fights Jansenists and parlements at home and Britain overseas. Genetics: continuity.

central.description: Frederick II’s seizure of Silesia (1740) sets Prussia against Austria for a generation. Maria Theresa survives the War of the Austrian Succession, wins Hungarian support at the 1741 Diet, and then reforms taxation and the army (Haugwitz, 1749). The Holy Roman Empire endures as a legal frame of hundreds of states; Bach dies in Leipzig in 1750. Genetics: continuity plus Danube resettlement.

scandinavia.description: Sweden, stripped of its Baltic empire in 1721, is ruled by its Riksdag parties (Hats and Caps) and loses more of Finland to Russia in 1743. Denmark–Norway is an absolute monarchy at peace, building Copenhagen’s Frederiksstaden. Linnaeus classifies the living world from Uppsala. Genetics: continuity.

italy.description: The 1748 peace freezes Italy: Bourbons in Naples–Sicily and Parma, Habsburgs in Milan, the Habsburg-Lorraine emperor in Tuscany, Savoy in Piedmont–Sardinia, with Venice, Genoa and the Papal States as old republics and a church state. Benedict XIV is a scholar-pope; Herculaneum and Pompeii are being dug up. Genetics: continuity.

balkans.description: After the 1739 Peace of Belgrade the Danube–Sava line is the border between Ottoman and Habsburg Europe. Wallachia and Moldavia are ruled by Phanariot Greek princes appointed from Istanbul; Constantine Mavrocordatos abolishes serfdom there in the 1740s. Serbs have fled north to the Habsburg Military Frontier. Genetics: continuity with frontier migration.

eastern.description: Empress Elizabeth’s Russia holds the Baltic provinces and the Hetmanate of left-bank Ukraine (restored under Kyrylo Rozumovsky in 1750). Poland–Lithuania, under the Saxon king Augustus III, is a large but weak noble republic. The Crimean Khanate and the Ottomans still hold the Black Sea coast. Genetics: continuity.

GBR.art: Hogarth’s moral series, Canaletto’s London views, Allan Ramsay’s portraits; Handel’s Messiah (1742) and Music for the Royal Fireworks (1749).
GBR.ideas: Mixed constitution, rule of Parliament, public credit and commercial empire. Excise and the Bank of England let a small island borrow cheaply for war.

images.alt: An Incident in the Rebellion of 1745 (Culloden) — David Morier
images.caption: An Incident in the Rebellion of 1745 (Culloden) — David Morier

GBR.literature: Fielding’s Tom Jones (1749), Richardson’s Clarissa (1748) and Samuel Johnson’s Dictionary (1755) shape the English novel and language.
GBR.philosophy: David Hume’s Enquiry concerning Human Understanding (1748); Francis Hutcheson and Adam Smith teach moral philosophy in Glasgow.
GBR.science: John Harrison’s marine timekeepers; James Bradley as Astronomer Royal; the 1752 switch to the Gregorian calendar. The Royal Society awards the Copley Medal to Benjamin Franklin (1753) for his electrical experiments.
GBR.story: In April 1746 the Duke of Cumberland’s army destroys Charles Edward Stuart’s Highlanders at Culloden. Within a few years the Highlands are disarmed, the old heritable jurisdictions abolished, and Britain turns its energy to the sea and the war for empire with France.

IRL.art: Georgian Dublin architecture; harp music after Turlough O’Carolan (d. 1738). Turlough O’Carolan’s harp tunes are collected and printed; Edward Lovett Pearce’s Parliament House introduces Palladian architecture on a monumental scale.
IRL.ideas: Ascendancy ‘patriot’ politics versus London’s control. Berkeley’s The Querist (1735–37) asks why a fertile country should be so poor, and proposes a national bank and home industry.
IRL.literature: Jonathan Swift (d. 1745) leaves Gulliver’s Travels and A Modest Proposal; Gaelic poets lament the fall of the old order. Swift’s Drapier’s Letters (1724–25) had made him a hero of Dublin’s Protestant ‘patriots’; Irish-language poets such as Aogán Ó Rathaille (d. 1729) mourn the fall of the Gaelic aristocracy in the aisling vision poem.
IRL.philosophy: George Berkeley, Bishop of Cloyne, and his immaterialism. Berkeley’s Treatise (1710) and Three Dialogues (1713) argued that to be is to be perceived; as bishop he writes on tar-water and Irish poverty.
IRL.science: The Dublin Society (founded 1731) promotes agriculture and industry. Trinity College Dublin, the country’s only university, is open in practice to Anglicans; the Dublin Society funds premiums for improved farming, linen and fisheries.
IRL.story: Handel’s Messiah has its first performance in Dublin in April 1742. The city is building squares and a parliament house worthy of a capital, while most Irish speakers outside it rent land they cannot own. Outside Dublin, the Penal Laws bar Catholics from Parliament, from most professions and from buying land on long leases, so the Catholic gentry that survived the seventeenth century shrinks year by year through conversion and subdivision.

FRA.art: Boucher, Chardin, Maurice-Quentin de La Tour; the Place Louis XV (today’s Place de la Concorde) planned in the 1750s. Madame de Pompadour patronises Boucher and the Sèvres porcelain works (moved to Sèvres in 1756).
FRA.ideas: Separation of powers, toleration, physiocracy. Quesnay’s Tableau économique (1758) founds the physiocrats’ economics.
FRA.literature: Voltaire’s Siècle de Louis XIV (1751); Rousseau’s Discourse on the Sciences and Arts (1750); Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws (1748).
FRA.science: Buffon’s Histoire naturelle (from 1749); Maupertuis’s Lapland expedition settled the Earth’s shape.
FRA.story: In 1751 Diderot and d’Alembert publish the first volume of the Encyclopédie. Within a year the royal council suppresses the first two volumes, and publication continues anyway—a sign of how far the reading public has grown beyond the court’s control. The volumes keep appearing until 1772, seventeen of text and eleven of plates, with articles by Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu and Quesnay.

ESP.art: The new Royal Palace of Madrid (from 1738); Domenico Scarlatti’s keyboard sonatas written in Madrid.
ESP.ideas: Reform from above: the Ensenada cadastre for a single tax. Regalism: the crown claims authority over the Spanish church, won in the Concordat of 1753.

images.alt: The Marqués de la Ensenada — Jacopo Amigoni, c. 1750
images.caption: The Marqués de la Ensenada — Jacopo Amigoni, c. 1750

images.alt: Farinelli and friends — Jacopo Amigoni, c. 1750–52
images.caption: Farinelli and friends — Jacopo Amigoni, c. 1750–52

ESP.literature: Benito Jerónimo Feijoo’s Teatro crítico universal and Cartas eruditas attack superstition. Ignacio de Luzán’s Poética (1737) pleads for neoclassical rules in Spanish drama.
ESP.philosophy: Feijoo’s critical empiricism. Feijoo, a Benedictine monk in Oviedo, publishes the Teatro crítico universal in eight volumes (1726–39) and the Cartas eruditas (1742–60), urging Spaniards to test beliefs against experience.
ESP.science: Jorge Juan and Antonio de Ulloa, veterans of the French geodesic mission to Peru; new naval arsenals. Jorge Juan and Ulloa’s reports of the geodesic mission (1748) are published in Madrid; Juan later studies British shipbuilding and modernises the Spanish dockyards.
ESP.story: Farinelli, the most famous singer in Europe, spends two decades at the Spanish court singing to calm Philip V and then directing opera for Ferdinand VI—an Italian voice at the heart of a French dynasty ruling Spain. Behind the music is policy: Ferdinand VI and his Portuguese queen, Barbara of Braganza, keep Spain out of war, settle the American border with Portugal and let Ensenada and Carvajal reform the state.

PRT.art: The palace-convent of Mafra; azulejo tile panels. Gilded woodcarving (talha dourada) and blue-and-white azulejo panels cover church walls; the Águas Livres aqueduct survives the earthquake.
PRT.ideas: Royal absolutism and economic nationalism. Pombal’s monopoly companies (the Douro wine company, 1756) regulate trade with Britain and Brazil.
PRT.literature: Luís António Verney’s O Verdadeiro Método de Estudar (1746) attacks Jesuit schooling. The Arcádia Lusitana (1756) gathers poets who want plain classical verse in place of the baroque conceit.
PRT.philosophy: Verney’s reforming pedagogy. Verney attacks Aristotelian teaching and calls for Portuguese grammar, modern logic and experimental physics.
PRT.science: The rebuilt Lisbon Baixa uses the gaiola, an anti-seismic timber cage. Pombal later reforms the University of Coimbra (1772) with laboratories and a botanical garden.
PRT.story: On 1 November 1755 an earthquake, fire and tsunami destroy much of Lisbon. Pombal’s reply—bury the dead, feed the living—and the rebuilding of the Baixa on a grid with earthquake-resistant frames make him the master of the state. Before the disaster, John V’s court had spent Brazilian gold on Mafra and on buying Rome’s favour; he was rewarded with the papal title ‘Most Faithful Majesty’ (1748). His death in July 1750 brings in his son Joseph I, who lets Carvalho e Melo run the government.

NLD.art: Delftware, Cornelis Troost’s comic scenes. Cornelis Troost (d. 1750), the ‘Dutch Hogarth’, paints theatre and comic scenes; Delft factories produce tin-glazed earthenware in imitation of Chinese porcelain.
NLD.ideas: Federal republicanism and toleration. The Orangist revolution of 1747–48 is the first sign of the Patriot–Orangist conflict that will split the republic in the 1780s.
NLD.literature: Dutch presses print what Paris bans: Amsterdam and Leiden publish much of the French Enlightenment. Elie Luzac and Marc-Michel Rey in Leiden and Amsterdam publish La Mettrie, Rousseau and others who cannot print freely in France.
NLD.philosophy: Hemsterhuis later; the republic of letters’ printing house. Leiden and Utrecht teach Newton through ’s Gravesande (d. 1742) and Musschenbroek, making the republic a channel for English science to the continent.
NLD.science: Pieter van Musschenbroek at Leiden builds the Leyden jar (1745–46). Musschenbroek’s Leyden jar is the first device to store an electric charge; its shock becomes the sensation of salons across Europe.
NLD.story: In 1747 French troops cross into Dutch Flanders and the provinces, in panic, make William IV hereditary stadtholder of all seven—ending the republic’s second stadtholderless period. William IV becomes stadtholder of all seven provinces in 1747, the first time one prince has held them all; the office is made hereditary in his line. When he dies in 1751 his son is three years old and the republic is governed by his widow and a guardian.

BEL.art: Grand Place guildhouses rebuilt after 1695; Rubens’s legacy in the churches. Brussels tapestry workshops still weave for European courts; the Coudenberg area is redesigned as Place Royale in the 1770s.
BEL.ideas: Provincial privileges defended against Vienna. Vienna’s ministers (Cobenzl, later Starhemberg) push cautious Catholic Enlightenment reforms; the provincial estates resist any loss of their charters.

images.alt: Charles Alexander of Lorraine — studio of Liotard
images.caption: Charles Alexander of Lorraine — studio of Liotard

images.alt: Palace of Charles of Lorraine, Brussels (from 1757)
images.caption: Palace of Charles of Lorraine, Brussels (from 1757)

BEL.literature: French-language court culture in Brussels; Flemish devotional print. Brussels printers and the Leuven faculty serve a Catholic, largely French-reading elite; Flemish is spoken in the countryside and the towns of Flanders and Brabant.
BEL.philosophy: Catholic scholarship at Leuven. Leuven remains loyal to Jansenist-tinged Augustinian theology even after the papal condemnations.
BEL.science: Leuven medicine and botany. Charles of Lorraine collects natural history and instruments; the Imperial and Royal Academy of Brussels follows in 1772.
BEL.story: After Fontenoy Marshal de Saxe takes the Netherlands fortress by fortress; at the peace of 1748 France hands them all back, a decision Parisians mocked as ‘bête comme la paix’—stupid as the peace. When the French withdraw, Charles of Lorraine returns to a country that has been fought over for a century. His governorship (1744–80) is remembered as a golden age: canals and roads are built, Ostend and Bruges are linked to the hinterland, and Brussels is rebuilt in a sober classicism.

DEU.art: Sanssouci rococo; Tiepolo’s Würzburg Residenz frescoes (1750–53); J. S. Bach dies in Leipzig in 1750.
DEU.ideas: Enlightened absolutism: ‘first servant of the state’. Frederick’s Anti-Machiavel (1740) and his reforms of torture and justice.
DEU.literature: Klopstock begins Der Messias (1748); Gottsched and Lessing reform German drama.
DEU.philosophy: Christian Wolff’s rationalism dominates German universities; Kant begins teaching in Königsberg in 1755.
DEU.science: Leonhard Euler at the Berlin Academy (1741–66); University of Göttingen (1737).
DEU.story: Frederick builds Sanssouci (1745–47) as a retreat ‘without care’, plays the flute for guests, invites Voltaire (1750–53), and keeps the largest army per head in Europe. In 1750 Voltaire arrives at Potsdam as Frederick’s guest; the friendship ends in a quarrel and his arrest in Frankfurt in 1753.

AUT.art: Schönbrunn rebuilt for Maria Theresa; Bellotto’s Vienna views (1758–61); Gluck’s early operas.

images.alt: Joseph II, heir to the reforms
images.caption: Joseph II, heir to the reforms

AUT.literature: Metastasio, imperial court poet in Vienna, writes the opera librettos the whole continent sets to music. Joseph von Sonnenfels and the Viennese press soon argue for a German-language Enlightenment.
AUT.philosophy: Catholic Enlightenment reform under Gerard van Swieten.
AUT.science: Van Swieten reforms medical teaching in Vienna. The Theresianum (1746) trains officials; Van Swieten modernises the court library and the University of Vienna’s medical faculty.
AUT.story: In 1756 Kaunitz achieves the ‘Diplomatic Revolution’: Austria allies with its old enemy France, while Britain sides with Prussia—a reversal meant to win Silesia back. The new course is meant to fight Prussia with Prussian methods: Kaunitz in diplomacy, Haugwitz in finance and Daun in the army, which wins at Kolín in 1757.

CZE.art: Kilian Ignaz Dientzenhofer’s churches, including St Nicholas in Prague’s Lesser Town. The Clementinum’s baroque library hall (1720s) and St Nicholas in the Lesser Town, finished in the 1750s, are high points of Prague baroque.
CZE.ideas: Bohemian estates losing ground to central government. The Theresian cadastre of 1748 records noble and peasant land for taxation.

images.alt: Maria Theresa, crowned Queen of Bohemia in 1743
images.caption: Maria Theresa, crowned Queen of Bohemia in 1743

images.alt: Dome of St Nicholas, Lesser Town, Prague
images.caption: Dome of St Nicholas, Lesser Town, Prague

images.alt: Baroque library hall of the Jesuit Clementinum
images.caption: Baroque library hall of the Jesuit Clementinum

images.alt: Prokop Diviš (19th-century portrait by Jan Vilímek)
images.caption: Prokop Diviš (19th-century portrait by Jan Vilímek)

CZE.literature: Czech literature survives in devotional and popular print. Jesuit hagiography and baroque hymnals (the Svatováclavský sborník) keep Czech in print; German is the language of administration and the universities.
CZE.philosophy: Jesuit Clementinum university culture. The Jesuit Clementinum dominates the Charles-Ferdinand University until the order is suppressed in 1773.
CZE.science: Prokop Diviš experiments with a lightning conductor (1754). Diviš, a Premonstratensian priest, raises his grounded ‘weather machine’ at Přímětice in Moravia on 15 June 1754; villagers later pull it down, blaming it for drought.
CZE.story: In 1741 the Elector of Bavaria is crowned King of Bohemia in Prague; two years later Maria Theresa takes the crown back and the Bohemian Court Chancellery is soon merged into Vienna’s central administration (1749). The reform hits the Bohemian nobility’s self-government but not its lordship over the peasants: the robot labour dues that tie Czech villages to their manors remain until 1848.

HUN.art: Esterházy palace at Fertőd (from 1720s, rebuilt 1760s). Baroque churches and palaces rise in Eger, Gödöllő (the Grassalkovich palace, from c. 1741) and Pressburg Castle, rebuilt for the queen.
HUN.ideas: Noble constitutionalism and tax exemption. The ‘Hungarian constitution’ means noble privilege: the Diet votes taxes on peasants only.

images.alt: Maria Theresa as Queen of Hungary
images.caption: Maria Theresa as Queen of Hungary

images.alt: Pressburg (Bratislava) Castle, seat of the 1741 Diet
images.caption: Pressburg (Bratislava) Castle, seat of the 1741 Diet

HUN.literature: Latin scholarship (Mátyás Bél’s survey of Hungary) and Hungarian verse. Mátyás Bél, a Lutheran pastor in Pressburg, publishes his Notitia Hungariae novae historico-geographica (1735–42), a county-by-county description of the kingdom in Latin.
HUN.philosophy: Catholic and Protestant colleges. Jesuit Nagyszombat (Trnava) university; the Reformed colleges of Debrecen and Sárospatak.
HUN.science: Mátyás Bél’s Notitia Hungariae novae. Bél’s survey also maps the kingdom’s mines, rivers and towns; Selmecbánya (Banská Štiavnica) mining school is founded in the 1760s.
HUN.story: At the Pressburg Diet of 1741 the Hungarian nobles answer Maria Theresa’s plea with ‘vitam et sanguinem’—our life and blood—and raise the troops that save her throne. The nobles’ loyalty has a price: the Diet of 1741 confirms their exemption from taxation and the separate Hungarian administration. Maria Theresa calls the Diet only twice more (1751 and 1764–65) and governs Hungary through decrees and the Hungarian Chancellery in Vienna.

CHE.art: Geneva enamelling and watchmaking. Watchmakers in the Jura and Geneva; Jean-Étienne Liotard, the Genevan pastellist, works across Europe.
CHE.ideas: Small-republic virtue and federal sovereignty. Jean-Jacques Burlamaqui’s Principes du droit naturel (1747) is read by later constitution makers.
CHE.literature: Albrecht von Haller’s poem Die Alpen (1729); Bodmer and Breitinger in Zurich. Haller’s Die Alpen praises the virtuous poverty of Alpine herdsmen; Bodmer translates Milton into German (1732).
CHE.philosophy: Rousseau; Burlamaqui’s natural law. Burlamaqui and later Vattel (The Law of Nations, 1758) give Swiss natural law a European audience.
CHE.science: Daniel Bernoulli’s Hydrodynamica (1738); Haller’s physiology. Daniel Bernoulli moves back to Basel in 1733; Haller, professor at Göttingen 1736–53, returns to Bern and writes his Elementa physiologiae (1757–66).
CHE.story: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, ‘citizen of Geneva’, wins the Dijon academy prize in 1750 by arguing that the arts and sciences have corrupted morals—fame begins with a Swiss republican scolding Paris. Rousseau’s prize essay is printed in Geneva’s shadow: the city, a Calvinist republic allied with the Confederacy, is itself divided between a ruling Petit Conseil and citizens who want more power.

ITA.art: Tiepolo, Canaletto, Piranesi’s Roman views; the Trevi Fountain (completed 1762); Caserta palace (from 1752).
ITA.ideas: Reforming ministers in Naples, Milan and Tuscany. Pietro Verri and Cesare Beccaria in Milan will turn this climate into On Crimes and Punishments (1764).
ITA.literature: Goldoni’s comedies in Venice; Metastasio’s librettos. Goldoni writes sixteen new comedies for the 1750–51 season in Venice; Metastasio works at the Vienna court.
ITA.philosophy: Giambattista Vico’s New Science (final edition 1744); Muratori. Antonio Genovesi takes the first European chair of political economy in Naples (1754).
ITA.science: Laura Bassi, professor of physics at Bologna; Agnesi’s calculus textbook (1748). Bassi, the first woman to hold a university chair in physics, teaches Newtonian experimental physics in Bologna.
ITA.story: Excavations begun at Herculaneum (1738) and Pompeii (1748) under Charles of Bourbon feed a European craze for antiquity that will become neoclassicism. Charles of Bourbon also builds the Teatro di San Carlo in Naples (1737), the Capodimonte palace and porcelain works, and begins the palace of Caserta in 1752 to Luigi Vanvitelli’s designs.

POL.art: Sarmatian coffin portraits; Saxon Palace in Warsaw. Saxon court architects in Warsaw; Bellotto, nephew of Canaletto, works in Dresden in the 1750s before moving to Warsaw in 1767.
POL.ideas: Golden Liberty versus reform. Golden Liberty (free election, liberum veto, the right of confederation) against Familia plans for a stronger executive.

images.alt: Józef Andrzej Załuski, co-founder of the Załuski Library
images.caption: Józef Andrzej Załuski, co-founder of the Załuski Library

images.alt: Warsaw from Praga — Bellotto (1770; Warsaw a generation later)
images.caption: Warsaw from Praga — Bellotto (1770; Warsaw a generation later)

POL.literature: Stanisław Konarski’s On the Means of Effective Counsel (1760–63) attacks the veto. Konarski’s Volumina Legum (from 1732) publishes the Commonwealth’s laws in print for the first time.
POL.philosophy: Konarski’s Piarist school reform. Piarist schools take on Locke and the new science; the Jesuit academies adapt.
POL.science: Załuski Library (1747). The Załuski brothers, both bishops, open their library to the public in 1747, with hundreds of thousands of volumes.
POL.story: Between 1736 and 1763 almost every Sejm is broken by a single deputy’s veto. The Załuski brothers open one of Europe’s first public libraries in Warsaw (1747) while the state cannot pass a budget. Konarski opens his Collegium Nobilium for young nobles in Warsaw in 1740, teaching modern languages, history and natural science: the first step towards the reforms of the 1760s–90s.

LTU.art: Vilnius baroque (Johann Christoph Glaubitz). Glaubitz rebuilds St Catherine’s and the Church of the Holy Spirit; the Radziwiłł court at Nieśwież has its own theatre.
LTU.ideas: Magnate republicanism. The Lithuanian magnates use the Commonwealth’s liberties against both king and Russia, but often in alliance with Russia.
LTU.literature: Polish-language noble culture; Lithuanian in catechisms and hymnals. The Lithuanian Lutheran pastor Kristijonas Donelaitis writes The Seasons (Metai, 1760s) in Prussian Lithuania.
LTU.philosophy: Jesuit Academy of Vilnius. The Jesuit Academy of Vilnius, the oldest university in the Commonwealth’s east (1579).
LTU.science: Vilnius Jesuit observatory (1753). The observatory of Vilnius University is founded in 1753, the oldest in the region.
LTU.story: Vilnius rebuilds its churches after the great fires of the 1740s in a late baroque that gives the city its skyline; in the same streets the Vilna Gaon becomes the leading rabbinic scholar of his age. Fires in 1737, 1748 and 1749 destroy much of Vilnius; the Jesuits, the Orthodox and the Uniate orders rebuild in the late baroque that gives the ‘Vilnius baroque’ school its name. Elijah ben Solomon, the Vilna Gaon, opposes the Hasidic movement spreading from Podolia.

UKR.art: Rastrelli’s St Andrew’s Church in Kyiv (1747–54). Cossack baroque churches with pear-shaped domes; the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra bell tower (1731–45).
UKR.ideas: Cossack autonomy and its erosion. The Hetmanate’s autonomy rests on Bohdan Khmelnytsky’s treaty of 1654, which Russia reinterprets as submission.

images.alt: Bakhchisaray, seat of the Crimean khans
images.caption: Bakhchisaray, seat of the Crimean khans

UKR.literature: Hryhorii Skovoroda, wandering philosopher-poet. Skovoroda studies at the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy and travels abroad (1745–50) before beginning his wandering life.
UKR.philosophy: Skovoroda. Skovoroda’s ethics of self-knowledge and ‘congenial labour’ are written down from the 1760s.
UKR.science: Kyiv-Mohyla Academy. The Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, with over a thousand students at its height, trains clergy and officials for the whole Russian Empire.
UKR.story: Kyrylo Rozumovsky, brother of Empress Elizabeth’s favourite, is elected hetman in 1750 at twenty-two, after the office had been vacant since 1734. He rules from Hlukhiv until Catherine II abolishes the hetmanate in 1764. In Hlukhiv the young hetman tries to restore Cossack courts and a capital fit for a court, and even plans a university in Baturyn; St Petersburg allows the pageantry but tightens its hold on taxes and appointments.

RUS.art: Rastrelli’s Winter Palace (1754–62), Smolny Convent and Catherine Palace. Ivan Argunov, a serf painter of the Sheremetevs, paints portraits; the Academy of Arts is founded in 1757.
RUS.ideas: Petrine state, noble service and serfdom. Noble privileges grow while serfdom deepens; the 1754 abolition of internal customs creates a single market.
RUS.literature: Lomonosov’s odes and Russian Grammar (1755); Sumarokov’s tragedies. Vasily Trediakovsky reforms Russian versification.
RUS.philosophy: Lomonosov. Lomonosov’s natural philosophy and his theory of Russian style (high, middle and low).
RUS.science: St Petersburg Academy of Sciences. The St Petersburg Academy (1724) employs Euler (to 1741 and again from 1766), Daniel Bernoulli and Lomonosov; the Academy’s expeditions map Siberia.
RUS.story: In 1755 Mikhail Lomonosov, a fisherman’s son from the White Sea, and Ivan Shuvalov found Moscow University. Lomonosov also writes the first scientific Russian grammar. Lomonosov is a chemist, a mosaicist and a poet: he sets up a glassworks for mosaics, writes odes to Elizabeth and argues with German academicians about the origins of the Russian state.

SWE.art: Drottningholm palace theatre (1766); Carl Hårleman’s interiors. Gustaf Lundberg’s pastels and the court rococo of Hårleman; Drottningholm’s palace and gardens.
SWE.ideas: Parliamentary rule by the estates. The 1766 Freedom of the Press Act, the first in the world, comes out of these Riksdag debates.
SWE.literature: Olof von Dalin’s weekly Then Swänska Argus. Hedvig Charlotta Nordenflycht, the first Swedish woman to live by her pen, publishes her poems from 1744.
SWE.philosophy: Swedenborg. Swedenborg turns from mining science to visions, publishing Arcana Coelestia (1749–56) in London.
SWE.science: Linnaeus; Anders Celsius’s temperature scale (1742). Celsius’s centigrade scale (1742), reversed after his death to its modern form; Christopher Polhem’s mechanics; Pehr Wargentin’s population statistics.
SWE.story: Carl Linnaeus publishes Species Plantarum in 1753, giving every plant a two-part name and sending his ‘apostles’ around the world to collect. Linnaeus’s pupils travel to China, Arabia, North America and Japan; Pehr Kalm goes to North America, Pehr Osbeck to China, Peter Forsskål to Arabia, and many never return.

FIN.art: Sveaborg fortress architecture. Ehrensvärd, also a draughtsman, designs the fortress gate and courtyards himself.
FIN.ideas: Frontier province of Sweden. Finland as the shield of the Swedish realm against Russia.

images.alt: Turku Cathedral, seat of Finland’s bishop
images.caption: Turku Cathedral, seat of Finland’s bishop

FIN.literature: Finnish in sermons and hymns; Swedish in print. Daniel Juslenius’s Finnish dictionary (1745) and patriotic histories praise the Finnish language.
FIN.philosophy: Academy of Turku (Åbo). The Academy of Turku, founded in 1640, teaches in Latin and Swedish; Henrik Gabriel Porthan begins his studies there in the 1750s.
FIN.science: Pehr Kalm, Linnaeus’s pupil, travels to North America (1748–51). Kalm, appointed professor at Turku, brings back North American plants and describes Niagara Falls in his Travels.
FIN.story: From 1748 Augustin Ehrensvärd builds the sea fortress of Sveaborg (Suomenlinna) off Helsinki to keep the Russian fleet out of Finland. The Swedish Diet of 1747 approves a plan for a great fortress and naval base off Helsinki and a frontier fortress at Degerby (Loviisa). Thousands of soldiers work on the islands; in 1750 the fortress is named Sveaborg, ‘Fortress of Sweden’. Sweden’s largest building project of the century is never quite finished.

DNK.art: Amalienborg (Nicolai Eigtved). Nicolai Eigtved’s rococo; Carl Gustaf Pilo, court painter.
DNK.ideas: Enlightened absolutism. The Royal Law of 1665 makes the king absolute; officials of the Danish chancellery and German Chancellery govern the realm.

images.alt: Amalienborg and Saly’s statue of Frederick V (unveiled 1771)
images.caption: Amalienborg and Saly’s statue of Frederick V (unveiled 1771)

DNK.literature: Ludvig Holberg’s comedies and histories. Holberg, born in Bergen and professor in Copenhagen, writes some thirty comedies for the Danish stage (Jeppe of the Hill, 1722) and is made a baron in 1747.
DNK.philosophy: Holberg. Holberg’s moral essays and his satirical novel Niels Klim (1741).
DNK.science: Royal Danish Academy of Sciences (1742). The Danish Academy of Sciences, founded in 1742, begins the mapping of the kingdom.
DNK.story: For the monarchy’s 300th jubilee in 1749 Frederick V lays out Frederiksstaden, a new district around four palaces at Amalienborg. Eigtved’s four Amalienborg palaces, built for noble families, frame an octagonal square; at its centre Moltke’s Asiatic Company pays for Jacques Saly’s equestrian statue of Frederick V, unveiled in 1771. Frederiks Church, planned at the same time, is completed only in 1894.

NOR.art: Rose painting (rosemaling) in farm interiors. Rose painting spreads through farm interiors from the mid-century; church woodcarving in acanthus style.
NOR.ideas: Union under Danish absolutism. Officials, merchants and farmers start to speak of Norway’s separate interests within the union.

images.alt: Bryggen, the merchant wharf of Bergen (rebuilt after 1702)
images.caption: Bryggen, the merchant wharf of Bergen (rebuilt after 1702)

NOR.literature: Holberg, born in Bergen. Pontoppidan’s Natural History of Norway (1752–53) describes fjords, sea serpents and the kraken.
NOR.philosophy: Holberg. Holberg’s Bergen birth gives Norway a share in the Dano-Norwegian Enlightenment.
NOR.science: Røros copper mines. Kongsberg silver mines, the largest industrial enterprise in the realm; Røros copper works.
NOR.story: The Strömstad treaty fixes the long Norwegian–Swedish border. The border treaty was signed in Strömstad on 21 September and 2 October 1751. Its first codicil, the Lapp Codicil, lets Sámi herders move their reindeer across the border in spring and autumn ‘according to ancient custom’, even in time of war—a clause still cited in border grazing disputes today.

TUR.art: Nuruosmaniye Mosque; Ahmed III’s fountain at the Topkapı gate. European motifs—acanthus, scrolls, curved cornices—appear on mosques and fountains; the Laleli mosque follows in 1760–63.
TUR.ideas: Ottoman order and military reform (Bonneval Pasha). Claude-Alexandre de Bonneval, a French convert, reorganises the bombardier corps (1730s).
TUR.literature: Divan poetry; Nedim’s Tulip-era verse. Müteferrika’s press prints histories, dictionaries and geographies until 1742; the poet Şeyh Galip is born in 1757.
TUR.philosophy: Islamic scholarship; Müteferrika’s printed books. Müteferrika’s own essay on the reform of the army and state (1732).
TUR.science: İbrahim Müteferrika’s press (1727). The press’s maps and Kâtip Çelebi’s geography Cihannüma (printed 1732).
TUR.story: The Nuruosmaniye Mosque (1748–55) is the first imperial mosque built in the Ottoman baroque—a style borrowed from Europe at the moment the empire stops losing to it. Mahmud I’s long peace in Europe lets the empire rebuild its capital, but the provinces are run by ayan families who collect taxes and raise their own troops.

GRC.art: Post-Byzantine icons. Post-Byzantine icon painting on Athos and in the Ionian school; British antiquaries Stuart and Revett draw the monuments of Athens (1751–53).
GRC.ideas: Greek Orthodox oikoumene. The Phanariot families of Constantinople serve the sultan as dragomans and princes of the Danubian principalities.

GRC.literature: Greek religious and scholarly print from Venice. Greek books are printed in Venice by the Glykis and Saros houses; Nikodemos the Hagiorite is born on Naxos in 1749.
GRC.philosophy: Voulgaris’s ‘Neohellenic Enlightenment’. Voulgaris teaches Descartes, Leibniz, Wolff and Locke alongside Aristotle.
GRC.science: Athonite Academy. The Athonite Academy’s mathematics and physics; Greek translations of Western textbooks.
GRC.story: In 1749 the Athonite Academy is founded on Mount Athos; under Eugenios Voulgaris (from 1753) it teaches Locke and Newton to Orthodox students. Voulgaris, born in Corfu and educated in Padua, gives the Academy a curriculum of classical philology, modern philosophy, mathematics and physics; conservative opposition forces him out in 1759, and he moves to the Patriarchal Academy in Constantinople.

ROU.art: Brâncovenesc style monasteries. Brâncovenesc architecture, after Constantin Brâncoveanu (d. 1714), at Horezu and in Bucharest’s monasteries.
ROU.ideas: Phanariot reform; Romanian estate claims in Transylvania. Micu-Klein petitions the Diet and Vienna to recognise Romanians as a fourth nation of Transylvania.
ROU.literature: Bishop Inochentie Micu-Klein argues for Transylvanian Romanians’ rights. Dimitrie Cantemir’s Descriptio Moldaviae (written 1714–16) and his history of the Ottoman Empire circulate in Europe.
ROU.philosophy: Princely academies at Bucharest and Iași. The princely academies at Bucharest and Iași teach in Greek.
ROU.science: Greek academies. Greek-language academies teach Aristotelian and, later, Newtonian natural philosophy.
ROU.story: Constantine Mavrocordatos abolishes serfdom in Wallachia (1746) and Moldavia (1749), turning serfs into peasants owing fixed labour dues—a reform decades before Vienna’s. The reform let peasants move between estates in exchange for a fixed fee and fixed labour days; it was meant to stop them fleeing across the mountains. In Transylvania, by contrast, Romanian peasants remain serfs and their Orthodox church is not recognised as one of the ‘received’ religions.

SRB.art: Fruška Gora monasteries. Žefarović’s engravings and frescoes; baroque iconostases in Karlovci and Novi Sad.
SRB.ideas: Habsburg privileges for Serb frontiersmen. The ‘Illyrian privileges’: Serbian self-government in religion and schooling within the Habsburg Monarchy.

SRB.literature: Church Slavonic in Russian redaction; Zaharija Orfelin later. Hristofor Žefarović’s engraved Stemmatographia (Vienna, 1741) celebrates the South Slav past; Zaharija Orfelin begins the Slaveno-Serbian Magazine in 1768.
SRB.philosophy: Church schools. Church schools in Karlovci teach Latin and Church Slavonic with Russian teachers.
SRB.science: Learning moves north with the migrants: Serbian schools at Sremski Karlovci (the gymnasium founded in 1791) grow from the church culture of the Habsburg Serbs. Learning moves north with the migrants.
SRB.story: In 1737–39 Patriarch Arsenije IV leads Serbs north across the Danube; the Metropolitanate of Karlovci becomes the centre of Serbian culture for a century. Arsenije IV’s flight in 1737–39 follows the first great migration of 1690 under Arsenije III. In the Habsburg lands, Karlovci becomes the seat of Serbian church and school life; the Cathedral of St Nicholas is built there in 1758–62.
